item.title: The Politics of Inclusion and Exclusion in Smart Cities
item.content:encoded:
This special issue examines the political dimensions of smart city development, focusing on how technological implementations shape patterns of inclusion and exclusion within urban environments. The call invites research that critically analyzes the social and political consequences of smart city initiatives.

Appel publié par Cities. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

  • June 30, 2027: Submission deadline

item.title: The Institutional Fragility of Inclusion in Contemporary HRM Systems
item.content:encoded:
Benjamin Laker, Henley Business School, University of Reading

Sven Horak, St. John's University

Toyin Ajibade Adisa, Royal Docks School of Business and Law, University of East London

Fulya Acikgoz, University of Sussex Business School

This special issue investigates how inclusion in human resource management has become institutionally fragile—endorsed in principle but inconsistently enacted or maintained symbolically without substantive commitment. It examines how identity is constructed, contested, and regulated through HRM practices when political, economic, organisational, and cultural pressures destabilise the systems that once supported inclusion.

The issue seeks theoretical, empirical, and methodological contributions that conceptualise inclusion as a dynamic process shaped by power, legitimacy, and resistance. Submissions should examine how HRM practices reinforce dominant norms, marginalise difference, or become sites of identity contestation. Contributions drawing on intersectionality, social identity theory, critical race theory, feminism, or postcolonial perspectives are particularly welcome, as are comparative studies exploring how inclusion operates across different institutional and cultural contexts.

Appel publié par The International Journal of Human Resource Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Institutional fragility of inclusion
  • Identity construction and negotiation in HRM
  • Symbolic inclusion versus substantive change
  • Performance systems and cultural fit criteria
  • Comparative and global inclusion analyses
  • HRM as voice suppression and identity masking
  • Intersectional identity effects on opportunity and recognition
  • Informal networks and shadow structures in inclusion
  • Organisational responses to erosion of inclusion mandates
  • Institutional logics and politics of belonging
  • Decolonial and Indigenous critiques of inclusion frameworks

Timeline

  • December 15, 2026: Manuscript deadline

item.title: Work, Intersectionality, and Neurodiversity: Understanding and Improving Inclusion Across the Career Span
item.content:encoded:
Debora Gottardello, University of Edinburgh

Narda R. Quigley, Villanova University

Susanne M. Bruyère, Cornell University

Neurodivergent adults, including those with autism, ADHD, dyslexia, and dyspraxia, encounter systemic barriers in employment such as recruitment difficulties, limited career progression, and retention issues, often leading to underemployment and premature career exits. These challenges are structural rather than incidental, as many workplace practices adhere to neurotypical norms, viewing cognitive differences as liabilities instead of diverse strengths requiring adaptive practices. Efforts towards inclusion frequently focus on early-career hiring and a single diagnostic category, usually autism, neglecting mid and late-career trajectories and the multifaceted nature of disadvantage. Single-axis approaches may overlook how compounded inequalities manifest within organizational contexts.

Appel publié par Journal of Managerial Psychology. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Intersectional patterns of inclusion, retention, progression and wellbeing across early, mid and later career stages for ageing neurodivergent workers
  • HR and line-management practices-recruitment, appraisal, promotion and leadership development; intersecting biases and evidence-based redesign for equity
  • Intersectional experiences of neurodivergence at work (e.g., ethnicity, gender, sexuality, class, migration status, age)
  • Physiological and health transitions in relation to neurodivergence (e.g., menopause, chronic conditions)
  • Late/retroactive diagnosis, professional identity, disclosure and workplace support; trajectories, risks and career consequences
  • Organisational culture, leadership and policy frameworks for neurodivergent inclusion, foregrounding intersecting identities and power dynamics
  • Cross-cultural and non-Western perspectives, including decolonial approaches, highlighting how local norms and colonial legacies shape intersecting experiences of neurodivergence at work
  • Comparative case studies of inclusion regimes and workplace adaptations across sectors and settings (including precarious/gig work), with attention to differential outcomes across intersecting identities
  • Participatory and co-produced approaches that centre multiply marginalised voices, with ethics and accessibility designed for intersectional needs
  • Sector-specific analyses (e.g., academia, public sector, technology, healthcare) specifying intersectional implications for policy and practice and for distinct workforce groups

Timeline

  • January 3, 2026: Opening date for manuscripts submissions
  • December 31, 2026: Closing date for manuscripts submission
